quote: Norges Bank should not have information about individuals' CBDC holdings or payments.
modality: normative 'should not' within a rough draft of design features
justification: Doc 6 says the design-feature list is only a rough draft, because Norges Bank concluded on 10 Dec 2025 that a CBDC is currently not warranted (doc 6 p.16, p.2). The statement says the central bank 'should not have information'. Under the contract, 'will not see/use' is not 'cannot link'. No document states that Norges Bank holds no routine key to identity in an adopted design. F1 therefore stays n/d, with an option-level claim recorded.
counter_evidence: doc 7 p.11: The solution is based on pseudonymity, which reduces the exposure of personal data during normal operation. However, this creates a structural privacy risk

quote: Banks are responsible for customer onboarding and for linking customers to ledger addresses that are registered in the banks’ own account registers.
actor: PSP (banks, distribution layer); payer and payee not distinguished
transaction_scope: online, retail CBDC sandbox (test case 1, Hyperledger Besu)
modality: tested capability in PoC sandbox only
justification: The inference is limited to the test case 1 retail sandbox, the same participant (the bank) and the same online mode, under §6.5. Premise (i): banks hold the link between customer and ledger address in their own account registers (doc 7 p.9). Premise (ii): participating banks have read access to the ledger's transaction history (doc 6 p.12). Premise (iii): banks can therefore attribute their customers' online transfers to persons. This is a tested sandbox capability, not an adopted design.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p.2: the introduction of either a retail or wholesale CBDC is currently not warranted

quote: KYC and AML checks of CBDC users would have to be performed by banks or other market participants that offer wallets for CBDC storage and transactions to their customers.
actor: PSP (banks/wallet providers) as holders; receiving authority not named
modality: AML/CFT obligations 'same as for other payment services'; suspicious-transaction reporting by third parties (doc 4 p.24); no specific legal process named
justification: Doc 6 assigns KYC/AML checks to banks and states that customer information remains with banks (doc 6 p.12, p.16). Doc 4 p.24 lists 'the reporting of suspicious transactions' among due-diligence tasks undertaken by third parties. Under the contract, a suspicion-based STR is a route via_PSP. All statements are option-level because no CBDC is adopted. Doc 5 p.15 notes that responsibility for transaction monitoring is legally unclear.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p.12: either through banks, court orders, technical leaks or data collocation – any participant with read access to the ledger would be able to view

quote: For example, it is possible that if the system permits anonymous payments, this functionality may be unavailable in offline situations.
justification: Offline functionality appears only as a desirable or required characteristic in the working-group reports (doc 2 p.18; doc 4 p.9, p.23). No adopted offline mode exists, and the privacy of transfers at synchronisation is not committed. Doc 4 even suggests anonymity may be unavailable offline. The 2025 decision not to introduce a CBDC is not a decision against offering offline. F4 is therefore n/d.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p.26: anonymous pre-paid cards can ensure anonymity within permitted quantitative limits

quote: Since this solution will also feature local storage, anonymous pre-paid cards can ensure anonymity within permitted quantitative limits.
transaction_scope: local storage / pre-paid card tier (closed account solution option)
justification: Lower-identification routes are mentioned only as options. These are anonymous pre-paid cards (doc 4 p.26) and limited access for tourists without full due diligence (doc 2 p.27-28). None is adopted. Because other routes are mentioned, the §6.6a inference of F7 = no is not available. F7 is therefore n/d.
counter_evidence: doc 2 p.27: consideration could be given to whether it should be possible to grant limited access to persons who do

quote: Know Your Customer (KYC), Countering the Financing of Terrorism (CTF) and Anti Money Laundering (AML) requirements for CBDC would be the same as for other payment services.
justification: Doc 6 states that KYC requirements would be the same as for other payment services, performed by banks or wallet providers. Doc 2 p.27 similarly ties access to the requirements for opening a Norwegian bank account. This is a rough-draft design feature after a decision not to issue a CBDC. It is therefore an option, not a commitment.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p.16: there is no basis for describing the design of a possible future CBDC solution

quote: If the ledger address of an end-user can be linked to an identity – either through banks, court orders, technical leaks or data collocation – any participant with read access to the ledger would be able to view the entire transaction history related to this address.
actor: any participant with ledger read access (CB, participating banks, others), once the link is supplied via banks or court order
modality: conditional on an address–identity link (e.g., court order via banks)
justification: The retail test case found that pseudonymous addresses can be attributed afterwards once linked to identity. Court orders and banks are named as linking channels. Pseudonymity then gives full retrospective access. This is a finding from a tested sandbox, not an adopted rule, so claim_status is tested.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p.40: keys can be generated so that authorised stakeholders can unlock information in accordance with specified procedures. Such solutions are in development.

quote: CBDC should not be programmable money, and programmability, if implemented, should be at the payment service level.
justification: Doc 6 rejects programmable money at the CBDC level and places any programmability at the payment-service level. Earlier working-group text discussed state-programmed social support only as a cautious possibility (doc 4 p.43). That was never a decision. Because no design is adopted, the value carries option status.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p.43: CBDC units used to pay various forms of social support may be programmed to be usable only in certain circumstances

quote: Norges Bank is assessing whether the introduction of a central bank digital currency (CBDC) is appropriate to ensure that the Norwegian krone remains an efficient, attractive and secure means of payment in the future.
justification: An efficient and secure payment system is the declared aim of the whole exploration (doc 4 p.4; doc 5 p.5; doc 6 p.2). The flag records a declared objective of the assessment. It is not an adopted CBDC.

quote: Introducing a retail CBDC is not a suitable measure for financial inclusion in Norway.
justification: Norges Bank explicitly rejects financial inclusion as a rationale for a Norwegian CBDC. Inclusion is cited only as an ECB motive. Earlier mentions of 'legal tender that can be used by anyone' describe attributes of cash, not a declared inclusion objective.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p.4: legal tender that can be used by anyone

quote: The two most important risks in Norges Bank's areas of responsibility are linked to currency substitution away from NOK and diminished national control over the payment system.
justification: The precautionary motivation explicitly concerns currency substitution away from NOK and national control over the payment system (doc 5 p.6). Doc 6 p.6 and p.8 say a retail CBDC could become relevant if national control is at risk.
counter_evidence: doc 1 p.7: The working group has not found arguments in these areas that provide an essential justification for introducing a CBDC.

quote: An independent backup for payment solutions based on bank deposits, a credit risk-free alternative to bank deposits that can foster competition in the payments market and legal tender that can be used by anyone.
justification: Declining cash use and the need for an independent back-up or contingency solution are declared motives throughout (doc 1 p.4; doc 2 p.6; doc 4 p.4). Doc 6 later judges contingency 'not a decisive argument'. That weakens the case but does not withdraw contingency as an assessed objective.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p.5: contingency considerations do not at present provide a decisive argument for the introduction of a retail CBDC

justification: No document declares AML/CFT or tax enforcement as an objective of a CBDC. AML appears only as a compliance requirement assigned to banks. The zero flag means 'not documented in the checked sources'.
counter_evidence: doc 1 p.18: On the other hand, lack of traceability can make it more difficult to discover certain crimes.

quote: Introducing a CBDC can be a way to ensure access to a means of settlement trusted by all, also in new payment arenas, and can also facilitate responsible innovation and improved payment contingency arrangements.
justification: The Governor's foreword lists responsible innovation as a reason to assess a CBDC. Competition in payments is a recurring purpose (doc 2 p.6-7). Doc 6 p.5 makes innovation in payment services one of the two points of particular emphasis.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p.5: Introducing a retail CBDC is not an appropriate measure at this stage to promote innovation

quote: Norges Bank has placed particular emphasis on whether the introduction of a CBDC could promote innovation in payment services and whether it would be a suitable instrument to strengthen contingency arrangements in Norway's payment system.
justification: The latest report places joint particular emphasis on two objectives: innovation in payment services and contingency. These sit under the overarching aim of an efficient and secure payment system. The 2018 preface named a single 'primary purpose' (confidence in money). The later framing replaces it with the joint emphasis.
counter_evidence: doc 1 p.4: The primary purpose of a CBDC is to ensure confidence in money and the monetary system.

value: innovation in payment services; contingency/back-up (under the aim of an efficient and secure payment system)
quote: Norges Bank has placed particular emphasis on whether the introduction of a CBDC could promote innovation in payment services and whether it would be a suitable instrument to strengthen contingency arrangements in Norway's payment system.
justification: These two objectives receive explicit 'particular emphasis' in the final Phase 5 report. They map to innovation_competitiveness and cash_substitute_resilience.
counter_evidence: doc 1 p.4: The primary purpose of a CBDC is to ensure confidence in money and the monetary system.

quote: The ledger for CBDC holdings and transactions should probably be based on blockchain technology.
modality: platform: Hyperledger Besu (retail), Hyperledger Fabric (wholesale), private Ethereum (Phase 4); sandbox/PoC only
justification: Testing used permissioned platforms (Hyperledger Besu and Fabric; private Ethereum in Phase 4), per doc 7 p.9, p.12 and doc 5 p.8. Doc 6 p.19 says a ledger should initially be private. Under the contract, a platform used only in a PoC is claim_status tested. No technology has been chosen, and no CBDC will be introduced at present.
counter_evidence: doc 5 p.10: we believe it is premature to draw a conclusion about which technological solution for the core infrastructure
